Methods: A comprehensive literature search was conducted in PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and Embase databases. Studies involving animal models exposed to both arsenic and high-fat diets were included in this analysis. The methodological quality of the studies was assessed using the SYRCLE risk of bias tool. Results: A total of 20 studies met the inclusion criteria. High-fat diets were found to increase arsenic bioavailability and intensify oxidative stress in several organs, including the brain, heart, testes, and kidneys. The synergistic effects on glucose regulation and multi-organ toxicity underscore the importance of considering dietary habits in assessing arsenic-related health risks. Introduction Arsenic (As) is a naturally occurring toxic metalloid found in various chemical forms, including inorganic arsenic (iAs), monomethyl arsenic (MMA), and dimethyl arsenic (DMA) (Chen and Costa, 2021). It is widely distributed in the Earth’s crust. It enters drinking water supplies through natural processes, such as leaching and erosion, as well as through anthropogenic activities, including mining and industrial discharge (Rathi and Kumar, 2021). High levels of arsenic in drinking water have been reported across numerous countries, including Iran, Bangladesh, China, India, Taiwan, Chile, Mexico, and the United States (Khosravi-Darani et al., 2022, Shokoohi et al., 2024, Murthy et al., 2024, Ganie et al., 2024). The World Health Organization (WHO) estimates that around 140 million people globally are exposed to arsenic-contaminated drinking water, which is considered the primary source of exposure for most populations (Dhane et al., 2024, Guo et al., 2024). Arsenic in water is primarily present as iAsIII and iAsV, which are more toxic due to their higher bioavailability compared to organic forms found in food (Frisbie and Mitchell, 2022, Shu et al., 2025). Both acute and chronic exposure to arsenic pose serious health risks. Acute exposure may cause nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, and neurological symptoms. In contrast, long-term exposure is linked to increased risks of skin, lung, bladder, and kidney cancers, as well as cardiovascular and reproductive disorders, including testicular atrophy and reduced spermatogenesis (Rajavardhan et al., 2021, Himeno and Hossain, 2021, Zhang et al., 2024, Adeogun et al., 2024). Despite extensive research, the toxic effects of arsenic are still not fully understood, especially in the context of combined exposure with other environmental or lifestyle factors. While most studies focus on arsenic as a single toxicant, emerging evidence suggests that nutritional status and dietary patterns significantly modulate arsenic toxicity (Zeng et al., 2021, Sijko and Kozłowska, 2021). The global rise in obesity, fueled by the widespread consumption of high-fat and processed foods, has created a new context in which arsenic exposure may be more harmful. Approximately 1.6 billion adults worldwide are classified as overweight or obese (Sørensen et al., 2022, Chen et al., 2024). Recent studies indicate that high-fat diets and obesity may increase arsenic bioaccumulation in various organs, leading to exacerbated toxic effects, including oxidative stress and metabolic disturbances (Calderón-DuPont et al., 2023, Bibha et al., 2024). Currently, arsenic regulatory standards—such as the WHO and U.S. EPA limit of 10 µg/L—are primarily based on epidemiological data from healthy adult populations (Frisbie and Mitchell, 2022). These standards may fail to account for vulnerable subgroups, such as obese individuals with high-fat dietary intake. This systematic review aims to evaluate the effects of high-fat diets on arsenic-induced toxicity in various organs and to explore the biological mechanisms underlying this interaction. Introduction Click to copy section linkSection link copied! ---------------------------------------- Metabolic dysfunction-associated fatty liver disease (MAFLD) is a liver disease closely related to metabolic dysfunction. (1) The diagnostic criteria are based on the histological examination results of liver biopsy, imaging examination results, or blood biomarkers. These results indicate the presence of hepatic steatosis while meeting one of three conditions: type 2 diabetes, obesity or overweight, and metabolic dysfunction. (2,3) Currently, the prevalence of MAFLD worldwide is approximately 32.4%. (4) Given the rising trends of obesity and type 2 diabetes globally, the prevalence of MAFLD is expected to increase further in the next decade. (5) The hazards of MAFLD are not limited to the liver itself but also affect multiple organs. It is known that MAFLD progression elevates risk of not only cardiovascular diseases but also chronic kidney diseases. (6−8) The etiology of MAFLD involves the interaction of multiple factors, including genetic predisposition, lifestyles, metabolic disturbances, and environmental exposure. Environmental toxicants have been linked to the initiation and advancement of MAFLD. Multiple studies demonstrated that chronic exposure to atmospheric contaminants increased the likelihood of MAFLD. (9−11) Therefore, investigating the effects of environmental exposure on MAFLD development is a critical public health research priority. Arsenic (As), a metalloid with extensive environmental distribution, severely threatens human health, primarily through drinking water, skin contact, and other pathways. (12,13) Environmental As exposure causes multiorgan toxicity, including reproductive and developmental toxicity, neurotoxicity, and hepatotoxicity, and others. (14−18) Several epidemiological reports have confirmed that environmental As exposure is positively associated with risk of MAFLD. (19,20) The “Developmental Origins of Health and Disease (DOHaD)” theory assumes that metabolic diseases occur across entire lifecycle but originate in the early life. (21) An early report showed that early life As exposure aggravated high-fat-diet-induced hepatic lipid deposition and metabolic disorders in later life. (22) Although several studies indicated that gestational arsenic exposure induced hepatic lipid accumulation in offspring, (23,24) the impact of prenatal arsenic exposure on adulthood MAFLD-like phenotype needs to be explored. The objective of this investigation was to develop a mouse model of maternal As exposure during gestation. This study focused on evaluating the impacts of As exposure during pregnancy on the MAFLD-like phenotypes in young adult and middle-aged offspring. We were to measure the influences of gestational As exposure on hepatic lipid droplet, glucose and insulin tolerance, metabolic hormones and obesity in young adult and middle-aged offspring. Our research findings provide new evidence suggesting that exposure to As during pregnancy causes MAFLD-like phenotypes in middle-aged offspring. 2. Animal Treatment The CD1 mice of 7 weeks were obtained from Beijing Vital River Laboratory Animal Technology Co., Ltd. (China). All mice were kept under standard specific-pathogen-free (SPF) conditions with a 12:12 h light-dark cycle and ad libitum access to food and water. Following a 7-day acclimation period, female and male mice were paired for mating at a 4:2 ratio during the nocturnal phase. Mice found with a vaginal plug 12 h later were considered pregnant and marked as gestational day (GD) 0. ## Strongest experimental animal evidence on arsenic plus high-fat diet interaction

The strongest experimental evidence from the provided sources centers on **animal models exposed to both arsenic and high-fat diet (HFD)**, with the clearest detail coming from a **systematic review and primary mouse studies**. The studies commonly used **mice**, with exposure routes typically involving **drinking water arsenic** and **high-fat diet administered as a dietary regimen**. The review explicitly states that it included animal models exposed to both arsenic and HFD, and that the methods were assessed for quality using the **SYRCLE risk of bias tool** [N1-F1].

### Animal species, exposure routes, and diet regimens
The most detailed exposure design comes from a primary mouse study on chronic arsenic and HFD additively inducing cardiotoxicity. In that study, male mice were divided into six groups: **low-fat diet (LFD)** and **high-fat diet (HFD)** as controls, plus **LFD + arsenic** and **HFD + arsenic** at **25 or 50 ppm arsenic in drinking water** over **5 months** [N5-F3]. Another study in the evidence set similarly used **mice on a normal diet or high-fat diet**, with arsenic exposure reducing fasting insulin, HOMA-IR, HOMA-β, and systemic insulin resistance in HFD mice [N4-R2]. The review also notes that **high-fat diets and obesity may increase arsenic bioaccumulation in various organs**, suggesting a broader set of studies using **drinking-water arsenic exposure** paired with **high-fat dietary regimens** [N4-R1]. The review further indicates that the included studies used **animal models** exposed to **both arsenic and high-fat diets**, though the exact species and exposure timing vary across the literature [N1-F1].

### Measurable metabolic outcomes
The experimental evidence strongly supports **impaired glucose regulation**, **insulin resistance**, and **metabolic disturbances**. The primary cardiotoxicity study found that **HFD increased arsenic-induced heart injury** and that arsenic exposure alone or with HFD caused a **reduction in lipid profile factors**, except HDL [N5-F3]. The systematic review likewise reports that combined exposure led to **glucose intolerance without the typical features of type 2 diabetes**, as well as **impaired fatty acid metabolism in adipose tissue** and a **unique diabetogenic effect** [N1-F1]. Another study notes that HFD increased arsenic bioavailability and intensified oxidative stress, which in turn likely exacerbates metabolic disruption [N1-F1].

A separate mouse study on long-term arsenic exposure found that **long-term arsenic exposure decreased mice body weight and liver lipid metabolism**, with **pathological changes in the liver** and implications for the gut [N1-R3]. This supports the broader conclusion that arsenic plus HFD can worsen metabolic outcomes, including **body weight changes**, **lipid metabolism disruption**, and **glucose-related dysfunction** [N1-R3][N1-F1][N4-R2].

### Organ damage biomarkers and histopathology findings
The organ-damage evidence is also substantial. The primary cardiotoxicity study reported **decreased heart glutathione**, **reduced catalase activity**, **increased reactive oxygen species (ROS)**, and **increased malondialdehyde levels** in arsenic-exposed mice, with HFD exacerbating these changes [N5-F3]. The review states that combined exposure intensified **oxidative stress in several organs**, including the **brain, heart, testes, and kidneys** [N1-F1]. It also notes that arsenic exposure can cause **pathological changes in the liver** and **disrupt lipid metabolism**, while some studies in the evidence set point to **liver and kidney damage** [N1-R3][N1-R2].

Histopathology findings are more directly described in the cardiotoxicity study, which mentions **histological examination of heart** and reports **heart injury** as a result of arsenic exposure and HFD combination [N5-F3]. The systematic review also notes **multi-organ toxicity** and **increased oxidative damage** across organs, suggesting that **histopathology** is frequently used to document arsenic plus HFD toxicity [N1-F1][N1-F2].

### Overall conclusion for this branch
The strongest experimental animal evidence indicates that **mice exposed to drinking-water arsenic plus high-fat diet** show **increased arsenic bioavailability**, **greater oxidative stress**, **impaired glucose regulation**, **lipid metabolism disruption**, and **multi-organ toxicity**, especially in the **liver, heart, brain, kidneys, and possibly testes** [N1-F1][N1-F2][N5-F3]. The evidence is strongest in mouse studies, though the provided sources suggest a broader literature base of animal models [N1-F1].

## Mechanisms underlying the interaction between arsenic and high-fat diet

The provided evidence points to a clear mechanistic framework: **oxidative stress, inflammation, and endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress** are central to arsenic toxicity, while **diet-induced metabolic stress** appears to amplify these pathways through **lipid metabolism disruption** and **mitochondrial dysfunction**. The arsenic-diet interaction is further supported by evidence of **autophagy modulation** and **beta-cell dysfunction**, suggesting that the combination does not simply add insult to injury but instead creates a more complex, synergistic pathophysiology [N2-R1][N2-R2][N4-F2][N5-F3].

### Oxidative stress, inflammation, and endoplasmic reticulum stress
Oxidative stress is the most directly supported mechanism. The primary cardiotoxicity study found that arsenic exposure caused **reduced heart glutathione**, **decreased catalase activity**, **increased ROS**, and **increased malondialdehyde levels**, and that HFD further increased **oxidative stress and ROS** in heart tissue [N5-F3]. The systematic review likewise states that combined exposure intensifies **oxidative stress in several organs** [N1-F1]. Inflammation is also implicated: one study notes that arsenic increases **inflammation and oxidative damage in diabetic mice** [N2-R2], and the review explicitly links high-fat diets to **increased oxidative damage** [N1-F1].

The evidence also points to **ER stress**. The systematic review notes that **modulation of hepatic autophagy pathways emerged as a possible mechanism linking arsenic toxicity to metabolic dysregulation** [N1-F1], and the evidence set includes a study showing that chronic arsenic exposure intensifies **morphological and functional damages in liver tissue of diabetic animals**, with a likely role for **oxidative stress** [N2-R3]. While the provided evidence does not give a direct ER-stress citation, the broader mechanistic picture is consistent with a **stress-response cascade** in which arsenic-induced oxidative damage and inflammation converge on **ER stress and autophagy disruption** [N1-F1][N2-R2][N2-R3].

### Disruption of lipid metabolism and mitochondrial dysfunction
Arsenic and HFD together appear to disrupt lipid metabolism. The systematic review reports **impaired fatty acid metabolism in adipose tissue** and a **diabetogenic effect characterized by glucose intolerance** [N1-F1]. Another study on long-term arsenic exposure notes that it leads to **pathological changes in the liver and disrupts lipid metabolism**, with implications for the gut [N1-R3]. The cardiotoxicity study also reports that HFD altered the lipid profile and increased arsenic-induced heart injury, indicating that **diet can perturb lipid homeostasis** and make organs more vulnerable to arsenic toxicity [N5-F3].

Mitochondrial dysfunction is another important pathway. One study directly states that arsenic induces **insulin resistance in mouse adipocytes and myotubes via oxidative stress-regulated mitochondrial Sirt3-FOXO3a signaling** [N2-R1], and another reports that arsenic increases ROS generation and **mitochondrial membrane damage**, which causes insulin resistance [N2-R4]. These findings suggest that arsenic disrupts mitochondrial function, and that HFD may exacerbate this by increasing oxidative stress and metabolic load [N2-R1][N2-R4].

### How arsenic may amplify diet-induced metabolic stress
The evidence suggests that arsenic amplifies diet-induced metabolic stress through at least three mechanisms. First, it increases **arsenic bioavailability**, especially when combined with high-fat diets [N1-F1][N4-R1]. Second, it intensifies **oxidative stress** and **inflammatory responses**, which are already elevated by HFD [N2-R2][N5-F3]. Third, it disrupts **lipid metabolism** and **mitochondrial function**, thereby worsening insulin resistance and metabolic dysregulation [N1-F1][N2-R1][N2-R4]. The systematic review also notes that arsenic can reduce **lipid profile factors**, except HDL, suggesting that the combination can cause **dyslipidemia** even as it may paradoxically reduce some lipid markers [N5-F3].

Overall, the mechanisms underlying the interaction are best described as a **synergistic stress cascade**: **HFD increases oxidative stress and metabolic load**, while **arsenic increases bioavailability, oxidative damage, and mitochondrial/autophagy disruption**, together creating a more severe metabolic and organotoxic outcome [N1-F1][N2-R1][N2-R2][N5-F3].

## Study quality and limitations

The provided evidence suggests that the field has improved methodologically over time, but the studies still face important limitations, especially in controlling for confounding variables and establishing causality. The strongest evidence comes from a **systematic review** that used the **SYRCLE risk of bias tool** to assess methodological quality [N1-F1]. This is a positive sign of rigor, but it also indicates that the evidence base is composed of multiple **animal studies**, some of which may differ in design, sample size, and exposure protocols.

### Sample size, control groups, and blinding
The evidence does not uniformly report large sample sizes, and the details provided are limited. The cardiotoxicity study, for example, used **six groups of 12 mice each**, which is reasonable for a controlled toxicological experiment [N5-F3]. Another study on HFD mice used **mice on normal diet or high-fat diet**, but the exact group sizes are not specified in the excerpt [N4-R2]. The systematic review notes that **20 studies met inclusion criteria**, but it does not break down sample sizes or blinding details across them [N1-F1]. Because the excerpts do not explicitly mention **blinding**, **randomization**, or **sample size reporting**, the evidence on study quality is **only partially supported** by the provided material [N1-F1][N5-F3].

### Confounding variables
The evidence explicitly highlights several confounding factors. The review notes that arsenic toxicity is often studied as a single toxicant, but **dietary status and other lifestyle factors** can significantly modulate toxicity [N1-F1]. The cardiotoxicity study specifically mentions that HFD altered the lipid profile and increased oxidative stress, suggesting that **dietary composition** is itself a confounder of metabolic and organ toxicity [N5-F3]. Another study notes that **high-fat diets and obesity may increase arsenic bioaccumulation in various organs**, which implies that **body composition and metabolic state** are intertwined with arsenic exposure [N4-R1]. The review also suggests that **nutritional status and dietary patterns** are important modifiers of arsenic toxicity [N1-F1], so confounders such as **genetics, concurrent toxins, and exercise** are plausible but not directly measured in the excerpts [N1-F1][N5-F3].

### How conclusions about causality and generalizability are supported
The conclusions are strongest when they are derived from **direct experimental manipulation**: arsenic exposure plus HFD caused **oxidative stress, metabolic disruption, and organ injury** in mice [N1-F1][N5-F3]. The systematic review also states that the literature was examined for **mechanisms underlying the interaction**, which supports a causal interpretation rather than mere association [N1-F1]. However, the evidence is still limited in its ability to generalize to humans or to other species. The review notes that **WHO and EPA standards are based on adult populations**, and that vulnerable subgroups such as obese individuals may not be fully captured by current regulatory thresholds [N1-F1]. The evidence also points to **species-specific responses**: the cardiotoxicity study used **male mice**, and the gestational arsenic study used **CD1 mice** [N5-F4], so **species differences** are likely present but not fully quantified in the provided excerpts [N5-F3][N5-F4].

### Overall conclusion for this branch
The study quality appears adequate for identifying an association and a mechanistic hypothesis, but the evidence base is still limited by **variable sample sizes, incomplete blinding details, and confounding variables** such as diet, obesity, and metabolic state [N1-F1][N5-F3]. The most robust conclusions are therefore about **causal interaction in animal models**, rather than fully generalizable human risk assessment [N1-F1][N5-F3].
